title: Children who rebelled
sum: The book opens with a heading (1:1) and then a courtroom. The LORD calls heaven and earth as witnesses against his own children, who know him less than an ox knows its owner (1:2–3). Judah is like a body beaten from head to foot, and its land like a country overrun; only a handful of survivors keep Jerusalem from the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah (1:4–9).

Then the LORD turns to Jerusalem's worship. He is sick of sacrifices, festivals and prayers from hands full of blood; what he wants is justice for the orphan and the widow (1:10–17). He offers terms: scarlet sins can become white as snow, but refusal means the sword (1:18–20).

A lament follows for the faithful town that has become a prostitute, with rulers who love bribes (1:21–23). The LORD will refine the city like silver, give it back honest judges and call it City of Righteousness (1:24–27), while rebels and those who worship at sacred oaks and gardens burn like dry tinder (1:28–31).
readings: Read as a covenant lawsuit

Many read the chapter as a trial: the LORD summons witnesses (1:2), states the charge (1:2–9), rejects the defense of offerings (1:10–15), sets out terms (1:16–20) and announces the verdict (1:21–31). On this reading the language of law runs through it: 'argue it out' (1:18), the orphan's rights and the widow's case (1:17, 23).
Read as the book's overture

Others read chapter 1 as a collection of separate oracles placed at the front because it sums up the whole book: rebellion, judgment, a remnant, the call to repent and the promise of a restored Zion. It shares many words with chapters 65–66, so the book begins and ends on the same notes (see 'The book's front door' below).

views.H: The picture of a land burned and overrun, with Jerusalem left 'like a city hemmed in' (1:7–8), best fits 701 BC, when Sennacherib of Assyria took forty-six walled towns of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage', as his own annals put it. Some date it instead to 734 BC, when Aram and Israel attacked Jerusalem (2 Kings 16:5). The charges of bribery and neglect of widows and orphans fit any decade of Isaiah's long ministry.
views.C: Most critical scholars see 1:2–31 as a collection of shorter oracles from different times in Isaiah's ministry, arranged as an introduction to the book. Fohrer called it a summary of Isaiah's message. Williamson and others argue that it was put in its present form late, perhaps when chapters 40–66 were joined to the book, since it shares so much vocabulary with chapters 65–66. The heading (1:1) is generally taken as an editor's.
views.J: Jewish communities read 1:1–27 as the haftarah on the Sabbath before the Ninth of Av, the fast for the destruction of the Temple; the Sabbath is called Shabbat Chazon after its first word, 'vision'. The verse 1:21, 'How (eikhah) has she turned into a prostitute', is chanted to the melody of Lamentations, which begins with the same word. The Talmud reads tsedaqah in 1:27 as 'charity': Jerusalem will be redeemed only through charity (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 139a).
views.X: Paul quotes 1:9 in the Greek's form, 'Had the Lord of Sabaoth not left us a seed' (Romans 9:29), for the remnant of Israel that believes. Christian writers from Justin Martyr on used 1:11–17 against the view that God needs sacrifices (Justin, First Apology 37). The offer of 1:18 has been one of the church's most-used invitations to repentance, read as God's promise to forgive through Christ.
views.F: The promise that Zion will again be called 'City of Righteousness, Faithful Town' (1:26) is read by many Christians, especially premillennial and dispensational readers, and by Jewish tradition, as still waiting: Jerusalem has not yet had judges 'as they were long ago'. On this reading the refining of 1:25 is part of a future purging before the Messiah's reign (compare Zechariah 13:8–9; Malachi 3:2–3).

deep.b:
For chapters 1–6 the Hebrew text is the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), read through the site's own Hebrew text, with its machine list of the codex's Ketiv and Qere readings. In these chapters that list has only three, at 3:15, 3:16 and 5:29, and none changes the sense.

The Qumran copies were read through the site's transcription of the Dead Sea Scrolls (the ETCBC edition by Abegg, Bowley and Cook): the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), which contains all six chapters, and the fragments 4QIsa-a (4Q55), 4QIsa-b (4Q56), 4QIsa-e (4Q59), 4QIsa-f (4Q60), 4QIsa-j (4Q63) and 4QpapIsa-p (4Q69), with the Murabba'at fragment Mur 3. Most of their differences are spelling; the ones that change the sense are given as variants. Where a scroll is broken, only the letters it preserves count as its reading.

The Greek is cited from Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. Where it matters, Ziegler's critical text is cited as reported by Ziegler and by the commentaries. The Targum is cited as translated by Chilton; the Latin Vulgate and the Syriac Peshitta are cited as reported by the commentaries named in each note.

Chapter 1 reads like a summary of everything that follows. Its themes run through the book: the LORD as 'the Holy One of Israel' (1:4), sin as rebellion of children against a father (1:2), worship that cannot replace justice (1:10–17), a remnant (1:9), the purging of Zion by fire (1:25) and its new name (1:26).

It also shares an unusual number of words with the last two chapters of the book. Heaven and earth are called in 1:2 and made new in 65:17 and 66:22. Those who 'rebelled against me' appear in 1:2 and in the book's last verse (66:24). The 'gardens' of idol worship in 1:29 return in 65:3 and 66:17. New Moon and Sabbath, rejected in 1:13–14, become the times when all people come to worship (66:23). The fire that no one puts out (1:31) is the fire that 'will not be put out' in 66:24. Many scholars think the editors who gave the book its final shape framed it this way on purpose, so that readers begin and end with the same choice.

Isaiah 1:11–15 is one of several prophetic passages that seem to reject worship outright (Amos 5:21–24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8; Jeremiah 7:21–23). Some older scholars took them as a rejection of the whole system of sacrifice in favor of a purely moral religion. Most now read them as a rejection of worship offered by people who do injustice: the problem is not the offerings but the 'hands full of blood' (1:15). Isaiah condemns prayer too (1:15), and no one thinks he opposed prayer. The same prophet sees the LORD in the Temple (6:1) and imagines all nations streaming to it (2:2–4; 56:7).

Psalm 51 makes the same point from the side of the worshiper: God does not want sacrifice without a broken spirit (Psalm 51:16–17), but the psalm ends with offerings on the altar (Psalm 51:19).

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:1; Deuteronomy 32:6; Romans 9:29; Amos 5:21–24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8; Psalm 51:7; Psalm 51:16–19; Revelation 7:14; Lamentations 1:1; Matthew 23:23; 65:17; 66:24

settings.to: Readers of the finished book
settings.when: when Isaiah's oracles were gathered into a book
settings.why: To name the prophet, his subject (Judah and Jerusalem) and the four kings in whose reigns he spoke, so that readers know the book is about real events in the 700s BC. Calling the whole book a 'vision' says that what follows is what the LORD showed Isaiah, not his own opinion.
settings.readers: Later readers in exile and after the return found the vision about Judah and Jerusalem addressed to them as heirs of that city.

settings.what: The LORD's charge against his children
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, with heaven and earth as witnesses
settings.when: after an invasion had left the countryside burned and Jerusalem cut off
settings.why: To make the people see their suffering as the result of rebellion against their own father, and to stop them from deceiving themselves: they have been beaten again and again and still do not turn. The survival of a handful (1:9) is mercy, not proof that all is well.
settings.readers: Readers after 586 BC, when Jerusalem fell, read the burned land and the few survivors as a picture of their own day.
views: Most scholars date it to 701, when Judah's towns fell and Jerusalem alone was spared (Wildberger; Williamson; Oswalt).
Some date it to the attack on Jerusalem by Aram and Israel (2 Kings 16:5).
A picture of judgment, not one event
Others read it as a general picture of covenant curses (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28) that need not match one invasion.

settings.what: Worship the LORD will not accept
settings.to: The rulers and people of Jerusalem, addressed as 'rulers of Sodom' and 'people of Gomorrah'
settings.when: probably at a festival in the Temple courts
settings.why: To tell worshipers that sacrifices, festivals and prayers are worthless to God when the same hands are full of blood. The oracle names what God wants instead: stop doing evil, seek justice, defend the orphan and the widow. Calling Jerusalem's rulers 'rulers of Sodom' is meant to shock.
settings.readers: Readers of every age have heard it as a warning against religion that leaves injustice alone.
views: Most take it as Isaiah's preaching at the Temple in the 700s BC.
Many see it as a separate oracle joined to 1:2–9 by the words Sodom and Gomorrah (1:9–10).

settings.to: The people of Jerusalem
settings.when: as the closing terms of the case
settings.why: To put the choice plainly: if they are willing and listen, sins red as dye can be made white and the land will feed them; if they refuse, the sword will feed on them. The offer is real, but so is the threat.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian readers alike have used 1:18 as an invitation to repentance and a promise of forgiveness.
views: Most read 1:18 as a real offer of cleansing (Oswalt; Motyer).
Some read it as a question, 'If your sins are scarlet, can they become white?', which expects the answer no (Wildberger, discussing older proposals).

settings.by: Isaiah: a lament, then the LORD's words
settings.to: Jerusalem and its rulers
settings.when: in a time of corrupt government in Jerusalem
settings.why: To mourn what Jerusalem has become, a city of killers and bribe-takers, and to announce that the LORD will refine it like silver, removing the dross and restoring honest judges. Judgment here is meant to purify the city, not to end it.
settings.readers: Readers after the exile saw the promise of 1:26 begin in the rebuilt Jerusalem, and many still wait for its full keeping.

settings.by: Isaiah (or a later voice in his book)
settings.to: People who worship at sacred trees and gardens
settings.when: unclear
settings.why: To warn those who look for life and fertility from sacred groves that they will become like a withered oak and a dry garden, and burn. The shift between 'you' and 'they' suggests separate sayings joined together.
settings.readers: Readers of the whole book link these verses with the garden worship condemned in 65:3 and 66:17.
views: Tree shrines were common in Judah in the 700s (2 Kings 16:4; Hosea 4:13).
Many scholars date them with 65–66, where the same practices are named (Blenkinsopp; Williamson).

title: The LORD's mountain
sum: A new heading (2:1) introduces a vision of the future. In the days to come the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above all mountains, and the nations will stream to it to learn his ways. He will judge between them, and they will beat their swords into plowshares and never again learn war (2:2–4). The house of Jacob is called to walk in that light now (2:5).

The rest of the chapter is the opposite picture. The land is full of fortune-tellers, silver and gold, horses and chariots, and idols (2:6–8). A day belongs to the LORD of Armies against everything proud and lofty: cedars and oaks, mountains and hills, towers, walls and ships (2:12–16). On that day people will throw their idols to the moles and bats and hide in caves from the dread of the LORD (2:18–21). A refrain marks the theme: human pride will be brought low, and the LORD alone will stand high (2:11, 17). The chapter ends with a warning: stop relying on human beings (2:22).
readings: Read as two pictures of the future

Many read the chapter as a deliberate pair: the nations climb the mountain to learn (2:2–4), while Judah, full of foreign gods and weapons, is brought down (2:6–22). The call of 2:5, 'let us walk in the LORD's light', links them: Israel should do now what the nations will one day do.
Read as a poem about pride

Others focus on 2:6–22 as a single poem on the day of the LORD, with its refrains (2:9, 11, 17; 2:10, 19, 21). On this reading the theme of the whole is height: only the LORD's mountain, and the LORD himself, will be high.

views.H: The wealth, horses, chariots and ships of 2:7 and 2:16 fit the prosperous years of Uzziah and Jotham, when Judah controlled the port of Elath on the Red Sea (2 Kings 14:22; 2 Chronicles 26:6–15). Deuteronomy warned kings against piling up horses, silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Foreign diviners and alliances (2:6) suggest the influence of Aram, Philistia and Assyria before the crisis of 734 BC.
views.C: Isaiah 2:2–4 appears almost word for word in Micah 4:1–3, and scholars debate who borrowed from whom, or whether both used an older song from the Temple. Many critical scholars date the oracle after the exile, when the hope of nations coming to Zion is common (56:6–8; 60; Zechariah 8:20–23); others defend a date in the 700s. In 2:6–22 the refrains are uneven, which suggests the poem grew over time; 2:22 is missing from the Greek.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 2:2–4 as a promise of the messianic age, when the nations will accept the God of Israel and war will end. Maimonides lists the end of war among the signs of the Messiah's days, while warning that the details cannot be known in advance (Mishneh Torah, Kings 11–12). The Mishnah records the sages' view, against Rabbi Eliezer, that weapons are a disgrace, not ornaments, since 2:4 says they will be done away with (Mishnah Shabbat 6:4).
views.X: Early Christian writers claimed 2:3–4 was being fulfilled as the gospel went out from Jerusalem and former enemies became peaceful. Justin Martyr wrote that Christians, once full of war, had changed their swords into plowshares (First Apology 39; Dialogue 110), and Irenaeus and Tertullian said the same. Revelation 6:15–16 echoes 2:19 in its picture of people hiding in caves from the face of God.
views.F: Premillennial and dispensational readers take 2:2–4 as a description of Christ's coming reign on earth from Jerusalem, when the nations will truly learn war no more; the church's growth has not ended war. Jewish hope likewise waits for the days of the Messiah. Others read the promise as being kept now in part, through the church, and fully in the new creation.

deep.b:
Isaiah 2:2–4 and Micah 4:1–3 are nearly identical. The differences are small: Micah has 'peoples' where Isaiah has 'nations' in the first verse and adds 'strong nations far away' in the third. Micah then adds a line Isaiah lacks, about each person sitting 'under his vine and under his fig tree, with no one to make them afraid' (Micah 4:4). Isaiah follows the oracle with a call to Israel (2:5), Micah with a contrast between the nations' gods and Israel's (Micah 4:5).

Three views are held. (1) Isaiah wrote it and Micah, his younger contemporary, quoted it. (2) Micah wrote it, since it fits the flow of Micah 3–4 better. (3) Both took it from a song already sung in Jerusalem's Temple. This site uses Isaiah's wording as the model for both books, and the differences will be given in a note in Micah.

The image of 2:4 has become one of the most quoted lines of the Bible. A bronze statue of a man beating a sword into a plowshare, by the Soviet sculptor Evgeny Vuchetich, was given to the United Nations in 1959 and stands in its garden in New York. The prophet Joel turns the image around in a call to war: 'Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning knives into spears' (Joel 3:10).

Isaiah does not say that the nations disarm by agreement. The peace comes because the LORD judges between them and settles their disputes (2:4), and because they first come to learn his ways (2:3). Without that teaching, the vision has no ground. Christians differ on how far it applies before the age to come (see 'Where Christians differ').

Amos is the first prophet known to speak of 'the day of the LORD', and he turned the phrase against Israel: it will be darkness, not light (Amos 5:18–20). Isaiah 2:12–22 is the first long poem on that day. Its target is not foreign nations but everything high: trees, mountains, towers, walls and ships, and the human pride they stand for. The refrain 'the LORD alone will stand high on that day' (2:11, 17) states the theme. Later prophets develop the picture (13:6–13; Joel 2; Zephaniah 1:14–18), and the New Testament uses it for the coming of Christ (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10).

echoes: Micah 4:1–5; Joel 3:10; Zechariah 8:20–23; Psalm 48:1–2; Psalm 122:1; Amos 5:18–20; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Revelation 6:15–16; Luke 23:30; Hosea 10:8; Luke 24:47; 56:7; 60:3

Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares

settings.to: Readers of the book
settings.when: when the oracles were collected
settings.why: To mark the start of a collection (often taken as chapters 2–4 or 2–12) and to claim it as the word Isaiah 'saw'. A second heading so soon after 1:1 suggests that chapter 1 was placed in front of an older collection.
settings.readers: It tells readers that the hope of 2:2–4 comes from the same prophet as the judgments around it.

settings.what: The nations climb the LORD's mountain
settings.by: Isaiah (the same oracle stands in Micah 4:1–3)
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, about the nations
settings.when: uncertain: in Isaiah's day or after the exile
settings.why: To promise that the small hill of Zion will become the center of the world, not by conquest but because the nations will want to learn the LORD's ways. Peace will follow his judgment. For Jerusalem's hearers it was both a hope and a rebuke: the nations would one day do what Israel was failing to do.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian readers have read it as the great promise of universal peace, and argued about when and how it comes.
views: Isaiah wrote it, perhaps early in his ministry, and Micah quoted it (Oswalt; Motyer; Wildberger; Roberts).
Both prophets drew on a song already sung in Jerusalem, in the language of the Zion psalms (Psalm 46; Psalm 48).
It was added to both books after the exile, when the nations' pilgrimage to Zion became a common hope (Blenkinsopp; Kaiser).

settings.what: A call to walk in the light
settings.by: Isaiah, or an editor linking the two oracles
settings.to: The house of Jacob
settings.when: as a bridge between 2:2–4 and 2:6–22
settings.why: To turn the vision into a call: if the nations will one day walk in the LORD's ways, Israel should start now. It echoes the nations' words in 2:3 ('let us walk').
settings.readers: Later readers took it as an invitation to live by the future now.

settings.what: The day of the LORD against all pride
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, rich and secure
settings.when: probably in the prosperous years of Uzziah and Jotham (before about 735 BC)
settings.why: To warn a wealthy, well-armed and religiously mixed society that its riches, weapons and idols would not save it on the day the LORD rises in terror. The refrains hammer one point: human height will be brought low, and the LORD alone will stand high.
settings.readers: Readers after 586 BC saw the fall of Jerusalem in it; the New Testament uses its language for the final judgment.
views: Most take 2:6–21 as Isaiah's early preaching, perhaps with later touches (Wildberger; Oswalt).
The uneven refrains and the prose of 2:20 suggest additions over time (Williamson; Blenkinsopp).

traditions.q: The nations 'will pound their swords into plowshares' (2:4). Must Christians refuse war now, or does that wait for the age to come?
views: War is never good in itself, and every citizen must work to avoid it, but governments may use force in legitimate defense when strict conditions are met: the harm must be lasting and grave, other means must have failed, success must be likely and the use of arms must not cause worse evils (the just war conditions, Catechism 2307–2309). The Catechism closes its teaching on peace by quoting 2:4 itself (Catechism 2317): the full peace it describes belongs to the Kingdom, toward which the Church works.

The Orthodox Church has never developed a formal just war teaching. War may at times be a tragic necessity in defense of the innocent, but it is never holy and always needs healing. Basil the Great advised that soldiers who had killed in war abstain from Communion for three years (Letter 188, canon 13), and many Orthodox writers take that as the Church's stance: killing, even when unavoidable, wounds the soul. The Russian Orthodox Church's Basis of the Social Concept (2000, section VIII) still allows a war of defense for one's neighbors and for justice, while calling war evil.

Christians may lawfully hold office, punish evildoers with the sword, engage in just wars and serve as soldiers (Augsburg Confession 16). God rules the world through government, which bears the sword; the peace of 2:4 is a gift of Christ's kingdom, not a law for the state.

Civil rulers may lawfully wage war 'upon just and necessary occasions' (Westminster Confession 23.2). Isaiah's vision describes the reign of Christ, which grows through the gospel and will be complete when he returns, but it does not take the sword from the magistrate before then.

The sword is ordained by God 'outside the perfection of Christ', and Christians are not to use it (Schleitheim Confession, article 6). Mennonites confess that the church is called to live now by the peace of the coming kingdom: Christians do not take part in war, but witness to the nations by refusing to learn war (Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective, article 22).

Friends declared to Charles II in 1660 that they 'utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end, or under any pretence whatever'. The Spirit of Christ, which leads into all truth, will never move them to fight; the peace of 2:4 begins in those who live by that Spirit now.

The verse describes Christ's thousand-year reign on earth after his return, when he will rule the nations from Jerusalem. It will be fulfilled to the letter then, and it is not a program for nations or the church in the present age, as the Scofield Reference Bible taught.

title: No one left to lead
sum: The LORD is about to take away everything Jerusalem leans on: its food and water, and then its leaders, soldiers, judges, prophets, elders and even its diviners (3:1–3). Boys will rule, neighbors will bully neighbors, and the young will sneer at the old (3:4–5). Things will be so bad that a man who owns a coat will be begged to rule over the ruins, and will refuse (3:6–7). Jerusalem has tripped because it defies the LORD as openly as Sodom (3:8–9). A short saying states the rule behind it: the righteous will eat the fruit of their deeds, and the wicked will get what they gave (3:10–11).

Then the LORD takes his place in court against the elders and officials who have grazed his vineyard bare and ground the faces of the poor (3:12–15). The last part of the chapter turns to the proud women of Jerusalem, who parade with their finery. The LORD will strip it all away: a long list of jewelry and clothes (3:18–23) gives way to rot, rope, shaved heads and sackcloth, while the men fall in battle and the city sits mourning in the dust (3:24–26).
readings: Read as political judgment

Many read the chapter as a portrait of a state collapsing from the top. When leaders are removed, chaos follows; when leaders rob the poor, God takes them to court. The women of 3:16–4:1 belong to the same ruling class whose luxury was paid for by the poor (3:14).
Read as a warning about pride

Others link the chapter with 2:6–22: the pride of men (2:11) and the pride of women (3:16) are both brought low. On this reading the theme is human self-reliance, announced in 2:22, 'Stop relying on human beings', and shown in the loss of every human support.

views.H: The removal of the elite (3:1–3) is what Assyria and later Babylon did to conquered nations: in 597 BC Babylon deported Jerusalem's soldiers, officials and craftsmen and left the poor (2 Kings 24:14–16). Boys on the throne (3:4) may hint at Ahaz, who came to the throne young (2 Kings 16:2). The wealth of Jerusalem's women (3:16–23) fits the prosperity of the mid-700s.
views.C: Most critical scholars see 3:1–15 as Isaiah's, with 3:10–11 as a wisdom saying added later. The prose list of 3:18–23 is often taken as an addition, since it breaks the poetry and begins 'On that day'. The poem on the women (3:16–17, 24) continues into 4:1, and the chapter break there is late.
views.J: The Targum and the rabbis read 3:10 as a promise to the righteous, 'it will be well with them', and the Talmud cites it in discussions of reward (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 40a). The list of finery in 3:18–23 was studied for the meaning of rare words; medieval commentators like Rashi and Kimchi explain each item from Aramaic and from the languages of their own day; Rashi often gives the Old French word.
views.X: The Greek of 3:10, 'Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us', was read by early Christians as a prophecy of the plot against Jesus (Justin, Dialogue 17; Epistle of Barnabas 6:7). Christian moralists used 3:16–24 against luxury in dress, and 1 Peter 3:3–4 makes a similar point more gently.
views.F: Some futurist readers see in the collapse of leadership in 3:1–7 a pattern that will be repeated at the end of the age, before the restoration of 4:2–6. Most readers, however, take chapter 3 as fulfilled in the sieges of Jerusalem in 701, 597 and 586 BC.

deep.b:
Isaiah 3:1–7 describes a world turned upside down. The supports a society leans on are removed one by one: food, water, soldiers, judges, prophets, elders, officials, skilled workers, and even the fortune-tellers people trusted. In their place come boys and 'spoiled children' (3:4), and the result is not freedom but bullying (3:5). The scene in 3:6–7, where a man is begged to rule because he still owns a coat and refuses because he has nothing, is the end of the line: no one wants power over a ruin.

The poem is not against youth as such. Its target is a society that has lost its wisdom because it has lost its fear of the LORD (3:8). Ecclesiastes 10:16 says the same: 'Woe to you, land, when your king is a boy'.

Isaiah 3:16–4:1 is often read as an attack on women, and it can sound harsh to modern ears. Several features matter for reading it fairly. The women are the wives and daughters of the ruling class whose crimes were just named (3:14–15): their jewelry is 'what you stole from the poor'. Their husbands are judged first (3:1–15) and die in battle (3:25). The punishment pictured, shaved heads, rope and sackcloth, is what happened to women when a city fell. Amos says much the same about the rich women of Samaria (Amos 4:1–3), and Isaiah returns to the theme in 32:9–14.

The list of 3:18–23 gives some twenty items of finery. Many of the words occur nowhere else, and every translation guesses at some of them; the site's Plain gives the most likely sense and the notes say where it is uncertain.

echoes: 2:22; 2 Kings 24:14–16; Ecclesiastes 10:16; Genesis 19:4–9; Proverbs 1:31; Galatians 6:7–8; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12; Amos 4:1–3; 1 Peter 3:3–4; 1 Timothy 2:9–10; Lamentations 1:1; 32:9–14

settings.to: Jerusalem and Judah
settings.when: in a time of weak or young rulers, perhaps early in Ahaz's reign
settings.why: To warn the city that the LORD is about to remove every human support it trusts, leaving chaos. The poem explains why: in word and deed Jerusalem defies the LORD and makes no attempt to hide it.
settings.readers: Readers after 597 and 586 BC, when Babylon deported the leaders and left the poor, read the list as fulfilled.
views: The young rulers of 3:4 may point to Ahaz's reign (Wildberger).
Others see a typical picture of collapse with no single king in view (Williamson).

settings.what: A saying about deeds and their fruit
settings.by: A wise teacher, perhaps an editor
settings.to: Readers of the book
settings.when: unclear
settings.why: To assure the righteous that in a judgment that falls on the whole city, God does not forget them, and to warn the wicked that they will get what they gave. It turns the oracle into a lesson.
settings.readers: It became a proof-text for reward and punishment in Jewish teaching, and in its Greek form a Christian proof-text for the Passion.

settings.by: Isaiah, then the LORD in his own voice
settings.to: The elders and officials of Jerusalem
settings.when: in Isaiah's ministry, probably early
settings.why: To put the leaders on trial for eating up the LORD's vineyard and crushing the poor. The LORD calls the people 'my people' twice, as their defender against their rulers.
settings.readers: Readers of 5:1–7 know already from 3:14 that the vineyard is Israel.

settings.by: Isaiah, with a prose list (3:18–23) that may be later
settings.to: Jerusalem, about the wealthy women of its ruling families
settings.when: in the prosperous years before the Assyrian crisis
settings.why: To announce that the luxury bought with the poor's goods will be stripped away when the city falls: the women will be shamed as captives and the men will die (the poem ends in 4:1).
settings.readers: Readers after 586 BC saw the city sitting in the dust (3:26) as Lamentations pictures it.
views: 3:16–4:1 is a single oracle by Isaiah, including the list (Oswalt).
The prose list of 3:18–23 and perhaps 4:1 were added later (Wildberger; Williamson).

title: Holy survivors under a canopy
sum: The chapter begins with the end of the poem of chapter 3: so many men have died that seven women beg one man to marry them, giving up their rights to food and clothing for the sake of his name (4:1).

Then, suddenly, comes a promise. On that day the LORD's branch will be beautiful and glorious, and the land's fruit will be the pride of Israel's survivors (4:2). Those left in Jerusalem will be called holy, written down for life, once the Lord has washed away the filth of Zion's daughters and the bloodshed of the city by a spirit of judgment and burning (4:3–4). Then the LORD will create over all of Mount Zion a cloud by day and fire by night, as in the wilderness, a canopy and a shelter from heat and storm (4:5–6).
readings: Read as hope after judgment

Many read 4:2–6 as the bright end of the collection that began in 2:1: it opens with the nations coming to Zion (2:2–4) and closes with Zion purified and sheltered (4:2–6), while judgment fills the middle. The pattern of judgment followed by hope is the book's pattern.
Read as a new exodus

Others focus on the cloud and fire (4:5), the booth (4:6) and the book of life (4:3): the survivors are a new wilderness generation, led and sheltered by God's presence. On this reading chapter 4 is one of the first glimpses of the new exodus of chapters 40–55.

views.H: The seven women of 4:1 reflect the losses of war: when an army fell, a city was left with widows (3:25). The promise of 4:2–6 was heard by survivors: the remnant left in Jerusalem after 701 BC, when only the city escaped, and again the returned exiles after 538 BC, who rebuilt in the ruins of the city.
views.C: Most critical scholars date 4:2–6 after the exile, for its language (bara' 'create', the book of life, a holy remnant) and its picture of a purified Zion, which fit the hopes of Persian-period Jerusalem. Others, especially conservative scholars such as Oswalt and Young, defend it as Isaiah's, noting that a remnant already appears in his son's name (7:3). The Greek has a different text in 4:2 and in 4:5, where it reads 'he will come' for 'he will create'.
views.J: The Targum reads 4:2 as 'In that time the Messiah of the LORD will be for joy and for glory', one of its messianic passages. Rabbinic midrash connected the canopy of 4:5 with the canopies God will make for the righteous in the world to come, each according to his honor (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 75a).
views.X: Many Christian readers, following the Targum's lead and the 'Branch' of Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12, have read 4:2 as a promise of Christ. The cleansing by 'a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning' (4:4) has been compared to John the Baptist's promise of baptism with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11).
views.F: Premillennial readers see 4:2–6 as the glory of Jerusalem in Christ's coming kingdom, when a visible cloud and fire will rest over Zion and the survivors of Israel will all be holy (compare Zechariah 14:20–21). Jewish tradition reads it of the messianic age. Others see its fullest form in the new Jerusalem of Revelation 21:3, where God's dwelling is with humanity.

deep.b:
The word tsemach, 'branch, sprout', is the center of a long debate. In Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 the LORD promises to raise up for David 'a righteous branch', and in Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12 'Branch' becomes a title for the coming leader. The Targum's 'Messiah of the LORD' in Isaiah 4:2 reads Isaiah in that light, and many Christian readers do the same.

Most modern commentators, however, read Isaiah 4:2 as the land's new growth after devastation: the parallel line, 'the fruit of the land', points that way, and Isaiah's own word for the coming king is different (choter, 'shoot', and netser, 'branch', 11:1). Some see both: the sprouting of the land and the coming of a king belong together in Isaiah's hope (11:1–9). The note on 4:2 sets out the readings.

deep.h: Judgment and hope side by side
deep.b: Isaiah's book often sets hope directly after judgment with no transition: 1:2–24 is followed by 1:25–27; 2:6–4:1 by 4:2–6; 6:1–13 ends with the holy seed. Readers have explained this in two ways. Some think the prophet himself always saw a remnant beyond the judgment, as the name of his son, 'A remnant will turn back' (7:3), suggests. Others think later editors added hopeful passages to older oracles of doom, so that the book would speak to those who had survived the disaster. Both views agree that the finished book wants its readers to hear the two together: judgment is not God's last word.

echoes: Exodus 13:21–22; Exodus 40:34–38; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Malachi 3:2–3; Matthew 3:11–12; Revelation 7:15–16; Revelation 21:3; Revelation 21:27

settings.to: Jerusalem, about its proud women
settings.when: looking ahead to a city emptied of men by war
settings.why: To complete the reversal of 3:16: the women who paraded will beg for a husband on any terms, to be spared the shame of widowhood and childlessness.
settings.readers: Readers of the book see in it the depth of loss after a siege.

settings.by: Isaiah, or a later voice in his book
settings.to: The survivors of Israel in Jerusalem
settings.when: uncertain: in Isaiah's day or after the exile
settings.why: To promise survivors that judgment will cleanse rather than destroy, and that the LORD will again dwell over Zion as he did in the wilderness, protecting all who gather there. It answers the despair of 3:25–4:1.
settings.readers: The returned exiles, few and poor, found here a promise that they were the holy remnant and that God's presence would return.
views: Isaiah expected a purified remnant from the start (Oswalt; Young; Motyer).
The language and hope of the passage belong to Persian-period Jerusalem (Wildberger; Williamson; Blenkinsopp).

title: The song of the vineyard
sum: Isaiah sings a love song about his friend's vineyard. The friend chose a fertile hill, cleared it, planted the best vines, built a tower and cut a wine vat, and it gave him stinking grapes (5:1–2). The friend himself asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge: what more could he have done? He will tear down its hedge and wall, let it run wild and forbid the clouds to rain on it (5:3–6). Only then is the vineyard named: it is Israel. God looked for justice and found bloodshed, for righteousness and heard an outcry (5:7).

Six woes follow. Woe to those who buy up house after house and field after field (5:8–10); to those who drink from dawn to dark and never notice what the LORD is doing, so that Sheol opens its mouth for them (5:11–17); to those who drag sin along and mock God's plan (5:18–19); to those who call evil good (5:20); to those wise in their own eyes (5:21); and to the heroes of drinking who take bribes (5:22–23). Fire will eat them like straw (5:24).

The chapter ends with the LORD's hand stretched out in anger (5:25) and a terrifying army summoned from the ends of the earth, tireless and unstoppable, roaring like a lion over its prey, until darkness covers the land (5:26–30).
readings: Read as a parable that traps its hearers

The song works like Nathan's parable to David (2 Samuel 12:1–7): the hearers are asked to judge a case and condemn themselves before they know it is about them. Read this way, the woes that follow are the evidence: the 'stinking grapes' are land-grabbing, drunkenness, corruption and bribery.
Read as a love song betrayed

Others stress the opening: Isaiah sings 'for my dear one', in the language of love songs (Song of Songs 8:11–12). The vineyard is not only a property but a beloved. On this reading the song is God's grief before it is his judgment, and the question of 5:4, 'Is there anything else I could do?', is the heart of it.

views.H: The woes fit the prosperity of Judah in the mid-700s, when land was concentrated in fewer hands and small farmers fell into debt (Micah 2:1–2; Amos 2:6). The army of 5:26–30 is Assyria, which under Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) became the first empire with a standing army and began its campaigns west. In 734–732 it reached Israel and Philistia, and in 701 it invaded Judah.
views.C: Most scholars take the vineyard song (5:1–7) and the woes (5:8–24) as Isaiah's. Since Duhm, many have argued that 5:25–30 belongs with the poem of 9:8–10:4, which has the same refrain, and that 10:1–4 is the missing seventh woe of chapter 5; the two were separated when Isaiah's memoir (6:1–9:7) was set between them. Others think the editors built the frame on purpose.
views.J: The Targum makes the vineyard allegory explicit: the LORD gave Israel an inheritance on a high hill, built his sanctuary among them and gave his altar to atone for their sins, but they did evil, and he will remove his Presence from them. The Tosefta reads the tower as the Temple and the wine vat as the altar (Tosefta Sukkah 3:15). 5:16 is read in the High Holy Day liturgy, where it is said that 'the holy God is made holy through righteousness'.
views.X: Jesus' parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1–12; Matthew 21:33–46; Luke 20:9–19) begins with Isaiah's vineyard and turns it against the leaders who reject the owner's son. John 15:1–8, where Jesus calls himself the true vine, may also draw on the song. Christian preachers have often used the woes against greed and corruption, and Paul's 'God justifies the ungodly' (Romans 4:5) has been read against 5:23.
views.F: The future song of the vineyard in 27:2–6, where the LORD guards his vineyard day and night and Israel fills the world with fruit, is read by many Christian and Jewish readers as still waiting, the reversal of 5:1–7. Futurist readers also see the army of 5:26–30 as a pattern for the gathering of the nations at the end of the age.

deep.b:
Jesus' parable of the wicked tenants opens with Isaiah's vineyard: "He set a hedge around it, dug a pit in it for a winepress and put up a tower" (Matthew 21:33). The hedge comes from the Greek of 5:2. In Jesus' story the fault lies not with the vines but with the tenants who will not give the owner his fruit and kill his son. The chief priests 'knew he had spoken the parable against them' (Mark 12:12). They may have known because Jewish readers already took the tower and wine vat of Isaiah 5 as the Temple and its altar, as the Targum and Tosefta Sukkah 3:15 do.

Isaiah's song blames the vineyard; Jesus' parable blames the leaders. Both end with the owner taking action: Isaiah's vineyard is abandoned, while Jesus' is given to others (Mark 12:9).

deep.h: Six woes, and a seventh in chapter 10
deep.b:
The word hoy, 'woe to', was the cry of mourners at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30; Jeremiah 22:18). The prophets used it to announce that those they addressed were as good as dead. Isaiah 5 has six: against land-grabbers (5:8), drinkers (5:11), those who mock God's plan (5:18), those who call evil good (5:20), those wise in their own eyes (5:21) and bribe-taking 'heroes' (5:22). A seventh, against those who write unjust laws, appears in 10:1–4.

Many scholars think it once stood here, and that 5:25–30, with its refrain about the LORD's outstretched hand, once ended the poem of 9:8–10:4. Others think the editors set the two passages around Isaiah's memoir on purpose. Either way, the finished book frames chapters 6–9 with judgment on Jerusalem's leaders and the threat of Assyria.

echoes: Song of Songs 8:11–12; 2 Samuel 12:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21; Mark 12:1–12; Matthew 21:33–46; Luke 20:9–19; John 15:1–8; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:1–3; Micah 2:1–2; Amos 6:1–7; Proverbs 3:7; Proverbs 17:15; 27:2–6; 9:8–10:4

settings.by: Isaiah, as a singer; the owner (the LORD) speaks in 5:3–6
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and the men of Judah
settings.when: perhaps at a vintage festival, when vineyard songs were sung
settings.why: To catch the hearers in their own judgment. They are asked to say what an owner should do with a vineyard that gives bad grapes after all his care, and then they learn that they are the vineyard. The closing wordplay (5:7) names the bad fruit: bloodshed instead of justice, a cry of distress instead of righteousness.
settings.readers: Jesus used the song against Jerusalem's leaders in his own day, and Christians have read it as a warning to the church.
views: Many date it to the beginning of Isaiah's ministry, before 735 BC (Wildberger).
A song for the feast of Booths
Some think it was sung at the autumn harvest festival in Jerusalem (Williamson discusses this).

settings.to: The landowners, drinkers, scoffers, clever men and corrupt judges of Jerusalem
settings.when: in the prosperous years of Uzziah and Jotham, or early under Ahaz
settings.why: To name the bad fruit of the vineyard one by one, and to announce what it will reap: empty houses, failed harvests, exile and death. The woes show that injustice is not an accident but a way of life the elite chose.
settings.readers: Readers in every age of inequality have heard 5:8 and 5:20 as addressed to them.

settings.to: Judah, about the coming empire
settings.when: as Assyria began to move west, from about 740 BC
settings.why: To warn that the LORD's anger has not run its course: after earthquake and death, he will whistle for a distant nation, an army no one can stop. The point is that Assyria comes at the LORD's call, so its coming is judgment, not chance.
settings.readers: Readers after 586 BC heard Babylon in it; the book itself names Assyria (7:17–20; 10:5).
views: It once ended the poem with the same refrain and was moved here (Duhm; Wildberger; Williamson).
The editors set it before chapter 6 to frame Isaiah's memoir with the threat of Assyria (Childs; Oswalt).

title: The vision in the temple
sum: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, the hem of his robe filling the Temple. Seraphim with six wings hover above him, calling to one another, 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies'; the doorways shake and smoke fills the house (6:1–4). Isaiah cries out that he is finished: a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips has seen the King (6:5). A seraph touches his mouth with a hot stone from the altar, and his guilt is taken away (6:6–7). When the Lord asks, 'Whom am I to send?', Isaiah answers, 'Here I am! Send me' (6:8).

The message he is given is the hardest in the Bible. He is to tell the people to listen and not understand, to make their hearts fat and their eyes shut, so that they will not turn and be healed (6:9–10). When he asks how long, the answer is: until the cities are ruined, the land empty and the people far away; and even the tenth that is left will be burned again, like a felled tree. Only the last line holds hope: the stump is a holy seed (6:11–13).
readings: Read as Isaiah's call

Many read chapter 6 as the account of how Isaiah became a prophet, like the calls of Moses (Exodus 3–4), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1) and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1–3). On this reading it stands here, after five chapters of preaching, to explain why his message met with such refusal: it was part of his commission from the start.
Read as a commission for a new task

Others note that Isaiah is already a prophet in chapters 1–5 and read chapter 6 as a commission for a particular task: to announce the hardening and the coming judgment in the crisis of 734 BC, which chapters 7–8 describe. On this reading chapter 6 opens Isaiah's memoir (6:1–9:7).

views.H: Uzziah died about 740 BC after a reign of some fifty years, the last of them as a man with a skin disease, living apart while his son governed (2 Kings 15:5; 2 Chronicles 26:21). Within a few years Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria was campaigning in Syria, and by 734 Aram and Israel were at war with Judah (2 Kings 16:5). The commission to announce judgment 'until the cities crash into ruins' (6:11) was kept in stages: the north in 722, Judah's countryside in 701, Jerusalem in 586.
views.C: Most scholars see 6:1–9:7 as an early collection, often called Isaiah's memoir, written in the first person and placed into the book later; chapter 6 opens it. They debate whether the vision was his first call or a later one, and whether the harsh commission of 6:9–10 was written after the fact, when the people had refused his message. 6:12–13 is often taken as a later expansion, and the last line of 6:13 is missing from the Greek.
views.J: The seraphim's song of 6:3 is the center of the Kedushah, said in the daily synagogue service, together with Ezekiel 3:12, and the Targum's expansion of it, 'holy in the highest heavens..., holy on earth..., holy forever and ever', is also used there. The Targum reads 6:1 as 'the year King Uzziah was struck' with skin disease, and Rashi explains 'died' the same way. Rashi, commenting on 1:1 and following the Mekhilta, takes chapter 6 as Isaiah's first prophecy, placed out of order. The Talmud tells that Manasseh used 6:1 against Isaiah, since Moses said no one can see God and live (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b).
views.X: John says Isaiah saw Christ's glory here (John 12:41), and many church fathers took the vision as one of the Son before his birth. The threefold 'holy' became the Sanctus of the Eucharist and was read as a hint of the Trinity. 6:9–10 is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts to explain why many did not believe in Jesus (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27).
views.F: Paul says that the hardening of Israel is partial and lasts 'until the full number of the Gentiles has come in', and then 'all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:25–26). Many Christians, especially premillennial readers, read the 'how long?' of 6:11 and the holy seed of 6:13 as pointing to a future turning of Israel. Jewish tradition reads the holy seed as the people that will survive every exile.

deep.h: Why the call comes in chapter 6
deep.b:
Jeremiah and Ezekiel begin with their calls; Isaiah's comes after five chapters. Three explanations are given. (1) The chapters are not in order. Rashi, in his comment on 1:1, says this was Isaiah's first prophecy, and many moderns agree that chapter 6 was his first call, placed here by the editors. (2) It is a second commission. Isaiah was already a prophet; in the year Uzziah died he was given a new and harder task. (3) It explains what came before. Chapters 1–5 show the people's refusal; chapter 6 shows that this refusal was foreseen and even announced in Isaiah's commission, so his failure is not God's failure.

Whatever the reason, the placing works: after five chapters of 'woe to them' (5:8–22), the prophet cries 'woe to me' (6:5). The judgment he announced falls first on himself, and he is cleansed before he is sent.

The vision has three movements. First the holiness of God: the King on his throne, the seraphim hiding their faces, the threefold 'holy', the shaking and the smoke (6:1–4). Then the response of a human being: not wonder but terror, because holiness exposes uncleanness (6:5). Then grace: fire from the altar touches the unclean lips, and guilt goes (6:6–7). Only after this does God ask for a messenger (6:8).

This order has shaped Jewish and Christian worship. The synagogue's Kedushah and the church's Sanctus repeat the seraphim's song. Many Christian liturgies place confession of sin near the start of worship, and the Orthodox liturgy uses the words of 6:7 at Communion. 'The Holy One of Israel', Isaiah's favorite name for God, comes from this vision: the holy God is Israel's God.

Isaiah 6:9–10 is one of the most troubling passages in the Bible: God seems to send his prophet to stop people from repenting. Ancient and modern readers have found several ways in. The Greek, followed by Matthew and Acts, turns the commands into descriptions: the people have closed their own eyes. Many read the commands as Hebrew irony, stating the result as if it were the goal: Isaiah's preaching will in fact harden them. Others speak of judicial hardening: after long refusal (1:2–5; 5:1–7), God confirms the people in the path they chose. All agree that 6:11–13 sets a limit: the hardening lasts 'until' the judgment, and a holy seed remains.

The New Testament writers used the passage to explain a painful fact, that many of Jesus' own people did not believe in him, without concluding that God had rejected them for good (Romans 11:1–2, 25–26). Christians differ on how God's action and human choice fit together here (see 'Where Christians differ').

echoes: 2 Chronicles 26:16–21; 1 Kings 22:19–23; Exodus 33:20; Ezekiel 1:26–28; Revelation 4:2–8; John 12:39–41; Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:11–12; Luke 8:10; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:7–10; Romans 11:25–26; Jeremiah 1:6–9; Exodus 4:10–13; Job 14:7–9; Ezra 9:2; 11:1; 52:13; 57:15

settings.what: The vision of the Lord on his throne
settings.to: Isaiah's disciples and the people of Jerusalem who heard him in the 730s, as the account that opens his memoir (6:1–8:18; 8:16)
settings.when: in the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC
settings.why: To tell how he came to speak for the LORD: he saw the holy King, was undone, was cleansed and volunteered. Telling it in the first person gives his hearers the reason to listen, and shows that the message comes from the throne of the universe at the moment Judah's throne fell empty.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian worship took up the seraphim's song, and many readers have heard 6:8 as their own call.
views: This was the start of his ministry, placed here by the editors (Rashi on 1:1; many moderns, such as Wildberger).
Isaiah was already a prophet; this is a commission for a new task (Oswalt discusses both; Young).
Isaiah wrote it down for the circle of disciples who kept his teaching after the people refused it (8:16).
He told it in Jerusalem to explain his authority and his harsh message (Williamson discusses both).

settings.by: The Lord, speaking to Isaiah; Isaiah's question in 6:11
settings.to: Isaiah, about 'this people'
settings.when: at the same vision
settings.why: To prepare the prophet for refusal: his preaching will make the people more deaf and blind, until judgment has emptied the land. The point is not that God wants them lost, but that the prophet must not mistake their refusal for his own failure, and must keep speaking 'until'. The holy seed (6:13) holds out a future beyond the judgment.
settings.readers: Exiles in Babylon heard the empty land and the people moved far away (6:12) as their own story; the New Testament writers heard in it the unbelief that met Jesus.
views: God told Isaiah at the start that his preaching would harden the people (Oswalt; Motyer).
Isaiah, or his disciples, described the call in the light of the refusal he met, especially in 734 BC (Wildberger; Williamson).

traditions.q: God tells Isaiah to make the people's hearts fat 'or else they may ... turn back, and be healed' (6:10). Does God harden people so that they cannot repent?
views: God predestines no one to go to hell; that requires a free turning away from God persisting to the end (Catechism 1037). In his eternal plan God includes each person's free response to his grace (Catechism 600). Thomas Aquinas teaches that God is not the cause of blindness and hardness of heart as he is of grace; he hardens by withholding grace from those who put an obstacle to it, as a just punishment (Summa Theologiae I–II, question 79, article 3). 6:10 is read in that light.

God's foreknowledge is not the cause of anyone's ruin; the cause is people's own will, which rejects the means God offers. When people long despise his word, God may harden them as a punishment, as he did Pharaoh, but he does not decree beforehand that they cannot repent (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI). Lutherans reject both the Reformed teaching of a decree of reprobation and any teaching that makes salvation depend on human choice.

God wills that all be saved. John of Damascus distinguishes God's first will, his good pleasure that all be saved, from his second will, his permission that those who refuse him suffer the result of their choice (Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 2.29). God foresees the hardening but does not cause it; the hardened heart is the sinner's own.

God in his just judgment passes by some, leaving them in the misery into which they have plunged themselves by their own fault, and hardens those he does not show mercy (Canons of Dort, First Head, articles 6 and 15; Romans 9:18). Calvin reads 6:10 as God blinding the people by the very preaching that should have saved them, as a punishment for their earlier contempt.

God's grace is 'free in all, and free for all', and no one is shut out from repentance by God's decree (John Wesley, Free Grace, 1739). 6:10 describes what happens when people refuse God's word: the word they reject leaves their hearts harder. It is the result of their refusal, not a decree that caused it.
